title: Juz 'Amma: The Short Surahs
intro: 38 days through Juz 'Amma, the Quran's thirtieth and final part, from An-Naba to An-Nas.

posts.caption: Juz 'Amma is the last of the Quran's 30 parts, named after the first word of An-Naba ("The Tidings"): 'amma, "about what". Its 37 short surahs, nearly all from Mecca, are the ones many Muslims learn first. An-Naba answers doubts about the Resurrection by pointing to everyday signs of care. Pickthall's "cloak" translates libas, the ordinary word for clothing.

An-Naba closes with this warning: a day is near when each person will see what their own hands "sent before", the deeds of their life. The disbeliever's cry, "Would that I were dust!", is regret at its deepest. Ibn Kathir records a view that animals, once judged among themselves, will be told to become dust, and that the disbeliever wishes he could share their fate.

An-Nazi'at ("Those Who Drag Forth") is a Meccan surah about the Resurrection. After describing the one who rebelled and chose the life of this world, it offers this contrast: whoever stood in awe of meeting their Lord and held their soul back from its desires will find the Garden their home. Pickthall's "lust" translates hawa, meaning whims and desires in general, and "the Garden" is Paradise.

posts.display: Let man consider his food: How We pour water in showers Then split the earth in clefts And cause the grain to grow therein.
posts.caption: Abasa ("He Frowned") is a Meccan surah. Here it invites the reader to look at an ordinary meal and trace it back: rain, split soil, growing grain. The list goes on through grapes, olives, dates and fruit, ending with "provision for you and your cattle".

posts.display: And when the girl-child that was buried alive is asked For what sin she was slain.
posts.caption: At-Takwir ("The Overthrowing") pictures the end of the world in a chain of "when" lines: the sun overthrown, the stars falling, the seas rising. Some pre-Islamic Arabs buried infant daughters alive. Here the girl herself is asked why she was killed, a question that falls on those who did it.

Al-Infitar ("The Cleaving") is a short Meccan surah about the sky splitting open at the end of time. In the middle comes this personal question. Al-Karim, "the Bountiful" or "the Generous", is one of the names of Allah, and the verse sets His generosity beside human carelessness.

posts.display_original: وَيْلٌ لِّلْمُطَفِّفِينَ ٱلَّذِينَ إِذَا ٱكْتَالُوا۟ عَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ يَسْتَوْفُونَ وَإِذَا كَالُوهُمْ أَو وَّزَنُوهُمْ يُخْسِرُونَ
posts.caption: Al-Mutaffifin means "the defrauders", those who give short measure. It is usually counted among the last Meccan surahs, though one early report links it to the markets of Medina when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ arrived there. It ties honest weights and measures to the Day of Judgment.

Al-Inshiqaq ("The Splitting") opens with the sky splitting at the end of time, then speaks to every human being. "Working toward thy Lord" renders kadih, a word for hard, steady toil. Life is pictured as a long labor that ends in meeting Allah.

Al-Buruj ("The Mansions of the Stars") recalls the "owners of the ditch", who burned believers for their faith. After that grim story comes this gentle description of Allah. Al-Wadud, "the Loving", appears as a divine name only twice in the Quran: here and in Surah Hud.

posts.display_original: وَٱلسَّمَآءِ وَٱلطَّارِقِ وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا ٱلطَّارِقُ ٱلنَّجْمُ ٱلثَّاقِبُ إِن كُلُّ نَفْسٍ لَّمَّا عَلَيْهَا حَافِظٌ
posts.caption: At-Tariq literally means "the one who comes by night", and the surah explains it as "the piercing star", which Pickthall calls the Morning Star. The oath leads to a quiet statement: every soul has a guardian over it. Many commentators understand the guardian as an angel.

posts.display: Praise the name of thy Lord the Most High, Who createth, then disposeth; Who measureth, then guideth.
posts.display_original: سَبِّحِ ٱسْمَ رَبِّكَ ٱلْأَعْلَى ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ وَٱلَّذِى قَدَّرَ فَهَدَىٰ
posts.caption: Al-A'la, "The Most High", opens with a call to glorify Allah and gives the reason: He creates and gives each thing its proper form, then sets its measure and guides it to its purpose. Muslims echo the opening in every prostration of prayer, saying subhana rabbiya al-a'la, "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High". According to well-known reports, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ often recited this Meccan surah in the Friday and Eid prayers.

Al-Ghashiyah ("The Overwhelming") describes the Day of Judgment, then turns to four things any traveller in Arabia knew well: the camel, the sky, the mountains and the open land. Each is offered as a sign worth looking at closely. Pickthall's "hills" here means mountains.

Al-Fajr ("The Dawn") is a Meccan surah. Here it describes a familiar human reaction: comfort feels like a mark of honor, hardship like a mark of rejection. The verse itself calls both a trial, and the next lines answer "Nay", turning to how the orphan and the poor are treated.

The last lines of Al-Fajr speak to an-nafs al-mutma'innah, "the soul at peace". After the turmoil of the Day of Judgment, this soul is called home, content and pleasing to its Lord. These verses are often quoted at times of death and mourning.

Al-Balad ("The City") opens with an oath by "this city", which commentators identify as Mecca. Here it lists gifts every person has: eyes to see, a tongue and lips to speak, and "the parting of the mountain ways". Many commentators read those two paths, an-najdayn, as the ways of good and evil.

Ash-Shams ("The Sun") opens with a chain of oaths: sun, moon, day, night, sky, earth, and finally the human soul, given an inner sense of wrong and right. Then comes the point of all those oaths: whoever purifies the soul and helps it grow succeeds, and whoever smothers it fails. "Causeth it to grow" translates zakkaha, from the same root as zakat; "stunteth" renders dassaha, to bury or smother.

Al-Layl ("The Night") contrasts the one who gives and is mindful of Allah with the one who hoards and feels self-sufficient. For the first it promises "the state of ease", al-yusra. Almost the same words appear in Al-A'la a few surahs earlier, addressed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

posts.display: By the morning hours And by the night when it is stillest, Thy Lord hath not forsaken thee nor doth He hate thee.
posts.display_original: وَٱلضُّحَىٰ وَٱلَّيْلِ إِذَا سَجَىٰ مَا وَدَّعَكَ رَبُّكَ وَمَا قَلَىٰ
posts.caption: Ad-Duha ("The Morning Hours") is one of the best-loved surahs of comfort. Classical commentators say it came after a pause in revelation, when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was distressed and some mocked that his Lord had abandoned him. It answers with an oath by the bright morning and the still night.

By most accounts, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was born after his father's death and lost his mother at about six; his grandfather and then his uncle Abu Talib raised him. Ad-Duha recalls that care. Commentators explain "wandering" as his life before revelation, not yet knowing the guidance that was to come. The surah then turns these gifts outward: to the orphan, to the one who asks, and to gratitude.

posts.display_original: أَلَمْ نَشْرَحْ لَكَ صَدْرَكَ وَوَضَعْنَا عَنكَ وِزْرَكَ ٱلَّذِىٓ أَنقَضَ ظَهْرَكَ وَرَفَعْنَا لَكَ ذِكْرَكَ
posts.caption: Ash-Sharh ("The Opening Up") is often read as a companion to Ad-Duha, continuing its comfort to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. "Caused thy bosom to dilate" means opened your heart, giving relief and calm. Commentators link "exalted thy fame" to his name being called out with Allah's in every call to prayer.

posts.display: By the fig and the olive, By Mount Sinai, And by this land made safe; Surely We created man of the best stature.
posts.display_original: وَٱلتِّينِ وَٱلزَّيْتُونِ وَطُورِ سِينِينَ وَهَٰذَا ٱلْبَلَدِ ٱلْأَمِينِ لَقَدْ خَلَقْنَا ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ فِىٓ أَحْسَنِ تَقْوِيمٍ
posts.caption: At-Tin ("The Fig") swears by the fig and the olive, Mount Sinai and Mecca, "this land made safe". Some commentators read the fig and olive as the land around Jerusalem and link the three places with the prophets Isa (Jesus) and Musa (Moses) and with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. The oaths lead to one claim: humans were created in the finest form.

posts.display_original: ٱقْرَأْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ خَلَقَ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ مِنْ عَلَقٍ ٱقْرَأْ وَرَبُّكَ ٱلْأَكْرَمُ ٱلَّذِى عَلَّمَ بِٱلْقَلَمِ عَلَّمَ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ مَا لَمْ يَعْلَمْ
posts.caption: By most accounts, these were the first verses revealed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, in the cave of Hira near Mecca around 610 CE, through the angel Jibril (Gabriel). Iqra means both "read" and "recite". Revelation begins with learning: the pen appears in the fourth verse.

Al-Bayyinah ("The Clear Proof") is usually classed as Medinan. This verse describes the reward of "those who believe and do good works" from the verse before. "Gardens of Eden" translates jannat 'adn, gardens of lasting home, and the pleasure it describes runs both ways.

Az-Zalzalah ("The Earthquake") describes the earth shaking and giving up its secrets at the end of time. It ends with two of the Quran's most quoted lines: no deed is too small to count, good or bad, and each will be seen again. Classical commentators explained dharrah, the "atom" here, as the smallest thing they could picture, such as a tiny ant or a speck of dust.

Al-Adiyat ("The Chargers") opens with a vivid scene of horses racing at dawn, snorting and striking sparks. Then it turns to its real subject: human ingratitude and the pull of wealth. Pickthall's "violent" renders shadid, meaning intense or fierce.

posts.display_original: ٱلْقَارِعَةُ مَا ٱلْقَارِعَةُ وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا ٱلْقَارِعَةُ يَوْمَ يَكُونُ ٱلنَّاسُ كَٱلْفَرَاشِ ٱلْمَبْثُوثِ وَتَكُونُ ٱلْجِبَالُ كَٱلْعِهْنِ ٱلْمَنفُوشِ
posts.caption: Al-Qari'ah means "the Striking" or "the Calamity", one of the Quran's names for the Day of Judgment. The repeated question builds suspense before two images: people scattered like moths, and mountains like tufts of carded wool. The surah then turns to the scales on which deeds are weighed.

At-Takathur means competing for more: more wealth, more children, more status. This short Meccan surah says such rivalry can absorb a whole life, right up to the grave. It ends by saying that every person will be asked about the blessings they enjoyed.

posts.display_original: وَٱلْعَصْرِ إِنَّ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ لَفِى خُسْرٍ إِلَّا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ وَعَمِلُوا۟ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ وَتَوَاصَوْا۟ بِٱلْحَقِّ وَتَوَاصَوْا۟ بِٱلصَّبْرِ
posts.caption: Al-Asr can mean "time", "the age" or "the late afternoon". In three verses it sums up what saves a person from loss: faith, good deeds, and urging one another to truth (haqq) and to patient endurance (sabr). Many Muslims learn it early and recite it often in prayer.

posts.display_original: وَيْلٌ لِّكُلِّ هُمَزَةٍ لُّمَزَةٍ ٱلَّذِى جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُۥ يَحْسَبُ أَنَّ مَالَهُۥٓ أَخْلَدَهُۥ
posts.caption: Al-Humazah means "the slanderer". This Meccan surah condemns two linked habits: belittling people behind their backs and to their faces, and hoarding wealth as if it could make a person live forever. Pickthall's "traducer" means someone who maligns others.

posts.display: Hast thou not seen how thy Lord dealt with the owners of the Elephant? Did He not bring their stratagem to naught, and send against them swarms of flying creatures, which pelted them with stones of baked clay.
posts.display_original: أَلَمْ تَرَ كَيْفَ فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ بِأَصْحَٰبِ ٱلْفِيلِ أَلَمْ يَجْعَلْ كَيْدَهُمْ فِى تَضْلِيلٍ وَأَرْسَلَ عَلَيْهِمْ طَيْرًا أَبَابِيلَ تَرْمِيهِم بِحِجَارَةٍ مِّن سِجِّيلٍ
posts.caption: Al-Fil ("The Elephant") recalls an event the people of Mecca knew well: an army led by Abraha, a ruler of Yemen, marched with an elephant to destroy the Kaaba and was turned back by flocks of birds pelting stones. The point for its first hearers was that Allah Himself had protected His House when they could not. Muslim tradition dates it to around 570 CE, the "Year of the Elephant", when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was born.

Quraysh was the tribe of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, keepers of the Kaaba in Mecca. Classical commentators explain that they ran trading caravans to Yemen in winter and to Syria in summer. The surah reminds them that their food and safety came from "the Lord of this House", the Kaaba.

Al-Ma'un is named for this surah's last word, "small kindnesses": everyday help such as lending a neighbor a pot or a bucket, as classical commentators explained. The surah opens with someone who pushes the orphan away, and here warns against prayer that is only for show.

According to classical commentators, some Meccan leaders offered the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ a compromise: worship their gods for a time, and they would worship his. Al-Kafirun ("The Disbelievers") is the reply, and it ends with this line, drawing a calm, clear line between two ways of worship.

posts.display_original: إِذَا جَآءَ نَصْرُ ٱللَّهِ وَٱلْفَتْحُ وَرَأَيْتَ ٱلنَّاسَ يَدْخُلُونَ فِى دِينِ ٱللَّهِ أَفْوَاجًا فَسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ وَٱسْتَغْفِرْهُ إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ تَوَّابًۢا
posts.caption: An-Nasr ("The Help") is a Medinan surah and among the last revealed. Commentators link "the triumph" with the opening of Mecca in 630 CE, after which whole tribes embraced Islam. At the height of success, the response it asks for is not pride but praise of Allah and seeking His forgiveness. Many, including Ibn Abbas, a cousin of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, understood it as a sign that his mission was nearly complete.

posts.display_original: تَبَّتْ يَدَآ أَبِى لَهَبٍ وَتَبَّ مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُۥ وَمَا كَسَبَ
posts.caption: Abu Lahab was an uncle of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and one of his fiercest opponents. According to well-known reports, when the Prophet ﷺ first called his clan to Islam, Abu Lahab cursed him, and this surah answers with the same word. Its point is that neither wealth nor close kinship to the Prophet ﷺ could save a man who set himself against the message. Al-Masad means "palm fibre", from its last verse.

posts.display_original: قُلْ هُوَ ٱللَّهُ أَحَدٌ ٱللَّهُ ٱلصَّمَدُ لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ وَلَمْ يَكُن لَّهُۥ كُفُوًا أَحَدٌۢ
posts.caption: Al-Ikhlas ("Sincerity") sums up tawhid, the oneness of Allah, in four short verses. As-Samad, "the eternally Besought", means the One on whom all depend. In a well-known hadith, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ described this surah as equal to a third of the Quran.

posts.display: Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the Daybreak From the evil of that which He created.
posts.display_original: قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ ٱلْفَلَقِ مِن شَرِّ مَا خَلَقَ
posts.caption: Al-Falaq ("The Daybreak") and the next surah, An-Nas, are known together as al-mu'awwidhatayn, "the two of seeking refuge". Both begin "Say: I seek refuge". Here refuge is sought in the Lord of the daybreak, who splits night into dawn, from every harm in creation.

posts.display_original: قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ ٱلنَّاسِ مَلِكِ ٱلنَّاسِ إِلَٰهِ ٱلنَّاسِ مِن شَرِّ ٱلْوَسْوَاسِ ٱلْخَنَّاسِ ٱلَّذِى يُوَسْوِسُ فِى صُدُورِ ٱلنَّاسِ مِنَ ٱلْجِنَّةِ وَٱلنَّاسِ
posts.caption: An-Nas ("Mankind") is the Quran's final surah, and it closes Juz 'Amma. It seeks refuge in Allah as Lord, King and God of humankind from the whisperer who plants evil suggestions in the heart. Many Muslims recite it with Al-Falaq and Al-Ikhlas morning and night. Thank you for reading along.
